---

## 3. What the hypothesis gets wrong

Point by point, because the coordinator asked for it plainly.

**1. "Calibration is closed form for every shape, no bisection."** *Half right.* It is closed form
for every arrow that **helps** a claim along, at every shape:
`added rate = [ln(1 − q0) − ln(1 − q1)] / (the arrow's shape added up over the window)`.
It is **not** automatically closed form for an arrow that holds a claim back, because such an arrow
cannot add a negative rate. The coordinator's own sketch — scale the rate by a factor raised to the
shape — needs a root find for an impulse or a ramp. I used a different scaling that **is** closed
form: the rate is multiplied by `1 − (1 − share) × shape`, which is the same thing at full strength
and interpolates linearly as the shape rises. It saturates: `30.0%` of the holding-back arrows in
the adversarial set could not hold back enough to reach their stated chance and were clamped at
"suppress the rate entirely while on" (`candidates_add.py`). The multiplicative form saturates too,
for the same reason — a cause cannot suppress a rate on days it is not on — but it saturates later,
which is where the two models are furthest apart (§4).

**2. "Cost proportional to causes × slices, not slices-to-the-power-of-causes."** *Right for the
causes that help, wrong in general.* Every arrow that holds a claim back multiplies the forward
pass by about the number of slices, because the rate is additive over helpers only *given* the
inhibitors' days. Measured: `.13 ms` per version per range with none, `.20 ms` with three on the
map, `.60 ms` with eight, `7.9 ms` with the generator's ten. **This is the one place the design can
still be made slow**, and it is why `inhibitors.py` matters.

**3. "The shape integrals do not depend on the version."** *Right, twice over.* Read off the
product: `_draw` takes `priors` and `strengths` and nothing else, `_version_priors` draws from
`claim.prior` and `_version_strengths` from `arrow.strength`
(`backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py`; the provenance spread in the evals worktree,
`feat-04b-evals/.../propagation.py:1509`, draws strengths only). No lag, shape or half-life is ever
redrawn. And measured: many versions in one pass equals one version at a time to **0.0**.

**4. "The winning sampler gets cheaper too."** *Wrong as first measured, right after one change.*
Reading the same arrays gave **355 ms** for 200 000 worlds against round one's **222 ms**, because
the survival chance had to be exponentiated once per world. Taking the exponentials once per
version up front — the rate adds over causes, so the survival chance is a *product*, and a product
of pre-exponentiated arrays needs no exponential at all — brings it to **215 ms**, and to **55 ms**
at the 50 000 worlds the accuracy actually needs. So the objection in round one §3 does go away,
but not for the reason given: it goes away because the sampler no longer needs the
slices-to-the-power-of-causes table in memory, not because reading it is cheaper.

**5. "It is *literally* Kent's decision R6."** *R6 is necessary, not sufficient.* R6 fixes what the
model is **asked** — the claim's chance with no cause on the map, and each arrow's chance with that
one cause at the start of the window. Both rates consume exactly those two numbers and reproduce
them exactly. R6 does not say how **two** causes combine, and that is the whole difference between
the two models. It is a separate decision and it is Kent's.

---

## 4. What the change of model moves — `model_diff.py`

**The worked example, for a finance reader.** A claim stands at 10% on its own. Two separate causes,
each of which *alone* would take it to 40% by the same deadline. Both happen on day one.

| | neither cause | one cause | **both causes** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **additive — independent routes** | .100 | .392 | **.590** |
| **multiplicative — round one** | .100 | .392 | **.910** |

*The additive number in words.* With no cause the claim fails 9 times in 10. One cause cuts that to
6 in 10 — so that cause removes a third of the ways it could fail. Two independent causes each
remove a third, so `.90 × (.60/.90) × (.60/.90) = .400` of the failure is left, and the claim
happens **.600** of the time. (The table reads `.590` rather than `.600` because the cause is placed
at the middle of the first slice rather than at day zero; both models show the same `.392` for one
cause, so the comparison is clean.)

*The multiplicative number in words.* Each cause multiplies the rate by about five; both together
multiply it by twenty-five. The claim reaches 91%.

**Which is right?** Neither, in general — it is a statement about the world. The additive form says
two causes are two separate ways for the same thing to happen, and knowing one has fired does not
make the other more potent. The multiplicative form says they reinforce. **What is not arguable is
that nobody stated the reinforcement**: the model is asked two numbers per arrow and neither of them
is about what happens when two causes coincide, so the amplification is put there by the engine's
choice of form and not by anything anyone said.

**What is lost.** Genuine reinforcement cannot be expressed. *"Hormuz reopens"* and *"OPEC+
restraint holds"* may really be worth more together than apart for Brent, and under the additive
rate they are not. The honest remedy if a map needs it is a named interaction term on the pair,
which is a third number to elicit — and nobody has priced whether a model can state it coherently.

**What is gained**, besides the cost: a claim's number can never be pushed past what its causes
severally justify, and the arithmetic is the familiar independent-routes rule a finance reader can
check by hand — as above.

**How far apart, across the set** (140 maps, both judged exactly, 24 slices, middle day; claims by
number of causes: 155 with none, 244 with one, 109 with two, 52 with three):

| every map — both choices at once | mean | median | 99th pct | worst | share > .05 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no edit (560) | .0060 | .0002 | .0688 | .1073 | 2.7% |
| *Suppose* (4 480) | .0051 | .0000 | .0902 | .3397 | 2.9% |
| *This happened* (4 480) | .0082 | .0003 | .1043 | .2437 | 4.4% |

Worst: trial 38, *Suppose* `c1`, read on `c2` — additive `.4559`, multiplicative `.1162`. That is an
**inhibitor** case, not a helper case: the multiplicative form suppresses far harder while a cause
is only partly on. Isolating the helper choice, on the 20 maps of 140 where every arrow helps:

| only maps where every arrow helps | mean | median | 99th pct | worst | share > .05 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no edit (80) | .0061 | .0004 | .0490 | .0634 | 1.2% |
| *Suppose* (640) | .0046 | .0000 | .0740 | .1809 | 2.0% |
| *This happened* (640) | .0088 | .0004 | .0870 | .1494 | 4.8% |

**So: two separate decisions, and the second is the louder one.** How helping causes combine moves
the median number by `.0004` and about 1 in 20 numbers by more than `.05`. How an arrow that holds a
claim back works moves the worst case to `.34`. A claim with one cause is identical under both, and
half the claims on these maps have one cause or none.

---

## 5. Does *This happened* still need the sampler, and can the correction be shared?

**Still needed.** The design's tables under the additive rate leave 5.36% of *This happened* numbers
off by more than `.005`, worst `.0420` (§2). Better than the `.2043` they left under the
multiplicative rate, and still not 99%.

**And the correction is now shareable, which it was not.** This closes round one's own open item.
Round one measured the correction's version-to-version movement only on easy maps and said plainly
that a map where the correction is large had never been checked. Trial 33 is that map
(`hardmap.py`, 200 versions each):

| trial 33, *This happened* on `c1`, read on `c3` | correction | how much it moves across versions | the answer's own spread |
|---|---|---|---|
| multiplicative rate, inputs drawn wide | .1172 | **.0805** | .1644 |
| multiplicative rate, inputs drawn narrow | .1732 | **.0544** | .0864 |
| **additive rate, inputs drawn wide** | **.0020** | **.0020** | .0748 |
| **additive rate, inputs drawn narrow** | **.0014** | **.0008** | .0323 |

Under the multiplicative rate, one correction shared across a whole range would have been wrong by
up to `.08` on a band end — **round one's assumption fails on exactly the map round one flagged.**
Under the additive rate it is `.002`, and sharing is honest. On three other hard maps the two rates
are closer (trial 65: `.0286` moving `.0121` against `.0210` moving `.0095`; trial 15 about equal;
trial 17: `.0194` moving `.0092` against `.0140` moving `.0062`), so the collapse on trial 33 is the
extreme, not the rule — but it is the case that decides whether the shortcut is allowed at all.

This is load-bearing for §2: the sample is a fixed 55 ms **because** it is taken once for a whole
range. If it had to be redone per version, 2 000 versions would cost 110 seconds.

---

## 6. What the decision record would have to say — sentences ready to paste

These are offered only if Kent takes the additive rate; nothing here is settled.

> **How two causes combine.** Each cause is an independent route by which the claim may come about:
> the causes add to the rate at which it happens, so the chance none of them brings it about is the
> product of the chances that none of them severally does. Two causes that each alone take a claim
> from 10% to 40% give 59% together, not 91%. Causes do not amplify one another; if a map needs
> that, it needs a third elicited number, and version one does not have one.

> **How an arrow that holds a claim back works.** It scales the rate down while it is on, in
> proportion to its shape, calibrated from its own stated chance. An arrow cannot hold a claim back
> on days it is not on, so a very strong one saturates; measured on the adversarial set, 30.0% of
> such arrows could not reach their stated chance and were clamped.

> **What it costs to compute.** A claim's table is an average taken one cause at a time, so a
> twenty-claim map with 2 000 versions takes 224 ms for the forward pass where the previous form
> took tens of seconds. An arrow that holds a claim back is the exception: it multiplies that claim's
> share of the cost by about the number of slices. Every real map checked carries at most one per
> claim.

> **Where the versions ride.** A version redraws only the stated chances, never a lag or a shape, so
> the shape integrals are computed once for a whole range and a version enters as a scalar.

---

## 7. What I did not check

- **The additive rate above four claims, for accuracy.** The judge is not computable there; the
  twenty-claim numbers are cost only.
- **The junction-tree solve** named in §2 as the nearest headroom. Not built, not measured.
- **A named interaction term** for two causes that genuinely reinforce (§4). Not built, and nobody
  has priced whether a model can state one coherently.
- **The exponential form of an arrow that holds a claim back** (`factor` raised to the shape), which
  is what the coordinator sketched. I measured the linear form instead, because it is closed form;
  the exponential one would need a root find and would saturate later, which is where §4's worst
  case comes from.
- **Whether real generated maps stay at one holding-back arrow per claim** once the prompt is
  changed to ask *what would stop this step* — which stack 05's freeze intends to do. Today's counts
  are from a prompt that never asks.
- **The `when` table under the additive rate.** Round one measured the arrival-day error under the
  multiplicative rate; the sampler's construction is unchanged, so it should carry over, but I did
  not re-run it.
- **The versions-per-range study under the additive rate.** Round one's 2 000 is used here as given.
  The band's width depends on the model, so the number could move.
- **I ran no test suite, no server, no browser and no paid call.** Nothing in the repository outside
  `plans/` was changed.

Nothing. This round wrote no product code and no chapter.

164	**Milliseconds.** `timing20.py`, on a map from `ve_cost.layered_dag(20, 3, seed=1000)`, one
165	observation in force, all twenty marginals. The first three rows are the *shared* pass every
166	candidate pays for before anyone asks a question.
167	
168	| | 1 version | 50 | 100 | 200 | 2 000 |
169	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
170	| calibrate the arrows | 28.0 | 95 | 192 | 384 | 3 905 |
171	| build the conditional tables | 12.9 | 628 | 1 217 | 2 438 | 24 831 |
172	| forward pass + yes/no tables | 0.9 | 14 | 28 | 56 | 570 |
173	| **shared by every candidate** | **41.8** | **737** | **1 437** | **2 879** | **29 318** |
174	| the exact yes/no solve, all marginals | 4.4 | 6.4 | 8.7 | 12.4 | 83 |
175	| **(b) total** | **46 ✓** | 744 | 1 446 | **2 891** | 29 401 |
176	| **(a) total, correction shared** | **161 ✓** | 856 | 1 555 | **3 002** | 29 527 |
177	| (a) total, correction redone per version | 161 ✓ | 6 367 | 12 340 | 24 992 | 281 761 |
178	| (c) per evidence day, every version | 101 ✓ | 3 709 | 7 406 | 14 611 | 152 022 |
179	
180	*All milliseconds, 12 slices, eight integration points per slice. ✓ = inside 300 ms.*
181	
182	At 24 slices — which §4 shows is the coarsest window worth having — the shared pass alone is
183	**208 ms for one version** and **9.6 s for fifty**.
184	
185	**So: no candidate passes.** The nearest miss is candidate (a) with the correction shared across
186	versions: **3.0 s at 200 versions and 12 slices, ten times the budget**. And the miss is not in the
187	sampler, which is 110 ms; it is in the 2.9 s of table-building that candidate (b) pays too.
188	
189	**What relaxing the criterion buys.**
190	
191	| relaxation | what it buys | what it costs |
192	|---|---|---|
193	| budget **3 s** for one world with its range | (a) passes at 12 slices, 200 versions | 12 slices is 2.5% of *This happened* numbers off by more than .005 against the continuous answer, even with the middle-day fix (§4) — so the accuracy half then fails |
194	| budget **12 s** | (a) passes at 24 slices, 200 versions, with both halves honest | a range takes twelve seconds |
195	| accuracy **.02 on 99%** | (b) passes accuracy: its 99th percentiles are .0046 / .0015 / .0151 | nothing on the clock — (b) is still 2.9 s at 200 versions. Relaxing accuracy alone does not help |
196	| **50 versions** instead of 200 | shared pass falls to 737 ms | the band's ends wander `.0498` — one significant figure |
197	| **one claim's number at a time**, no range | 46 ms (b) / 161 ms (a) — both pass | there is no range, which is the product's honesty feature |
198	
199	**The cheapest thing that has not been tried.** The tables are built by enumerating every
200	combination of the causes' arrival slices — 2 006 900 entries for this map at 24 slices — and then
201	*averaging* them. An average does not need every point. Replacing the enumeration with five
202	quadrature points per cause cuts it to 31 375 entries (64× fewer) and the whole forward pass from
203	208 ms to **38.5 ms** per version. It costs accuracy: *This happened* goes from 5.68% to 9.27% off
204	by more than .005, and no edit from 1.25% to 2.92% (`quad.py`, 60 maps). **And it is not available
205	to the winning candidate**, because a weighted forward sample needs a claim's table at whatever day
206	its causes actually landed on, not at five chosen days.
207	
208	---
209	
210	## 4. The grid nobody chose — the largest single number in this report
211	
212	Every measurement above compares candidates *on the same grid*, so it is a fair comparison. But the
213	grid itself carries an error that the judge and every candidate share, and it is bigger than the
214	thing this spike was sent to measure.
215	
216	A cause that arrives anywhere inside a slice has to be given a day. `rt_core` gives it the slice's
217	**last** day. That is late by half a slice on average — 1.25 days at 24 slices on a 60-day window.
218	
219	Against a fine reference (60 slices, middle day), 10 maps, every query (`convergence.py`,
220	`midpoint.py`):
221	
222	| the engine's window | *This happened*: 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
223	|---|---|---|---|
224	| 12 slices, arrival at the slice's last day | .0547 | .0668 | 44.7% |
225	| 24 slices, last day | .0240 | .0290 | 27.8% |
226	| 60 slices, last day | .0093 | .0111 | 8.1% |
227	| **12 slices, arrival at the slice's middle** | .0068 | .0085 | 2.5% |
228	| **24 slices, middle** | **.0018** | **.0027** | **0.00%** |
229	
230	**Twelve slices with the middle-day convention beats sixty slices with the last-day one, at a
231	twentieth of the cost.** This is a one-line change (`spike_core.representative_days`) and it costs
232	nothing.
233	
234	It does **not** change which candidate wins. Re-run at 24 slices, middle day, judged there
235	(`midpoint.py`, 140 maps): the design's tables are still 6.07% off by more than .005 on *This
236	happened*, worst `.2095`; the sample with the control variate is still 0.00%, worst `.0021`. The
237	two defects are independent, and both are real.
238	
239	*One caveat, honestly.* The *Suppose this is true* row of the grid comparison (5.6% over .005 at 24
240	slices middle day) is an artefact of this harness, not of the model: a supposition pins the claim
241	to the first slice, whose representative day differs between grids. A real implementation would pin
242	it to day zero. It is listed under what I did not check.
243	
244	---
245	
246	## 5. The worst remaining case, drawn
247	
248	Trial 33 of the adversarial set is where the design is worst, and it is exactly the shape the red
249	team named: the observed claim is also a cause of another cause, and the reach is through impulse
250	arrows (`worst_case.py`).
251	
252	```
253	   c0  ── deadline day 8.5, own chance .54
254	    │
255	    ├──► c1  deadline day 20.3, own chance .07
256	    │        from c0: .11 if that cause alone happens, lag 5.2 d, step
257	    │
258	    ├──► c2  deadline day 43.4, own chance .10
259	    │        from c0: .61, lag 3.1 d, step
260	    │        from c1: .33, lag 2.5 d, IMPULSE half-life 5.7 d
261	    │
262	    └──► c3  deadline day 56.0, own chance .09
263	             from c0: .11, lag 18.2 d, IMPULSE half-life 4.6 d
264	             from c2: .91, lag  5.2 d, IMPULSE half-life 12.4 d
265	             from c1: .03, lag 16.1 d, IMPULSE half-life 13.5 d
266	```
267	
268	*This happened: `c1` is true.*
269	
270	| | c0 | c1 | c2 | **c3** | worst gap |
271	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
272	| judge (exact over times) | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | **.6155** | — |
273	| (b) prior-timing tables | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7269 | **.4112** | **.2043** |
274	| (c) widen the observed claim | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7282 | .4187 | .1968 |
275	| (c) widen it and its causes | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | .4192 | .1963 |
276	| (c) per evidence day | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7282 | .6076 | .0079 |
277	| (c) widen everything read | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | .6155 | .0000 |
278	| (a) sample 200 000, corrected | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7278 | .6159 | **.0005** |
279	
280	Twenty points of probability, on the claim furthest downstream — the kind of claim a trade sits on.
281	The design prints `.41` where the answer is `.62`.
282	
283	**The worst case candidate (a) has left** is not structural: trial 21, *This happened* on `c0`, read
284	on `c2` — judge `.4807`, sample `.4821`, gap `.0020` at 200 000 worlds, and it shrinks as the square
285	root of the count. **The worst case candidate (c) widened has left** is trial 124, gap `.0063`, and
286	it does not shrink with anything.
287	
288	---
289	
290	## 6. How many versions a range needs
291	
292	`versions.py`. Twenty thousand versions of the twenty-claim map are solved exactly under an
293	observation; that pool stands in for "all versions". Then each smaller count is drawn from it two
294	thousand times and the band recomputed. *Wander* is half the middle 90% of where an end lands.
295	
296	**Uncertain inputs drawn wide (a typical band .254 across):**
297	
298	| versions | worst end wanders | as a share of the band | share of band ends inside .005 |
299	|---|---|---|---|
300	| 50 | .0498 | 18% | 22.9% |
301	| 100 | .0390 | 14% | 29.6% |
302	| 200 | .0275 | 10% | 38.8% |
303	| 500 | .0176 | 6% | 55.6% |
304	| **2 000** | **.0086** | **3%** | **83.9%** |
305	
306	**Uncertain inputs drawn narrow (a typical band .115 across):**
307	
308	| versions | worst end wanders | as a share of the band | share inside .005 |
309	|---|---|---|---|
310	| 50 | .0252 | 16% | 41.0% |
311	| 100 | .0192 | 12% | 53.0% |
312	| 200 | .0133 | 9% | 67.7% |
313	| 500 | .0086 | 6% | 86.5% |
314	| **2 000** | **.0046** | **3%** | **99.2%** |
315	
316	**Recommendation: keep 2 000.** It is the smallest count that holds a narrow band's ends to two
317	significant figures, and even it does not hold a wide band's — a band `.25` across needs about
318	**6 000** versions for that, by the square-root rule the table obeys. The engine analyst's proposal
319	of "about 200 versions" is **wrong by an order of magnitude**: at 200 versions the 5th and 95th
320	ends wander by a tenth of the band's own width, which is one significant figure. The inner eight
321	worlds do go away — that saving is real — but it does not buy a smaller outer loop.
322	
323	**Can the correction for *This happened* be shared across versions?** Yes, and it is the only thing
324	that makes candidate (a) affordable at all. On 8 maps × 200 versions, with the exact correction
325	(judge minus the design's answer) computed per version:
326	
327	| | mean | 90th pct | worst |
328	|---|---|---|---|
329	| how big the correction is | .0005 | .0019 | .0041 |
330	| how much it moves from version to version (sd) | .0008 | .0025 | .0071 |
331	| how much the answer itself moves (sd) | .0616 | .1107 | .1234 |
332	| the ratio of those two | .011 | .030 | .096 |
333	
334	The correction moves about **1% as much as the answer does**. Sharing one sampled correction across
335	every version adds about `.0013` to a band end on average and `.0117` at its worst. That is the
336	trade: one sample instead of two hundred, for a hundredth of an extra error on most numbers and a
337	tail that needs watching on maps where the correction is large. **These eight maps are four claims
338	each and the correction is small on them by construction** — on a map shaped like trial 33 the
339	correction is `.20`, and 1% of that is `.002`, still small, but nobody has measured the version-to-
340	version movement of a correction that size.
341	
342	**Cost per version, and therefore per range** (candidate (a), 12 slices, shared correction):
343	2 879 ms of shared pass + 12 ms of solve for 200 versions + 110 ms for one sample = **3 002 ms**.
344	Per version that is 14.4 ms, and the sample is a fixed 110 ms however many versions there are.
345	
346	---
347	
348	## 7. The times the trade will read
349	
350	Stack 06 reads a sample of worlds as `when` (the day each claim first came true, −1 for never) plus
351	a `weight`. Under *This happened* those days are only right if whatever produced them is. Red team
352	S2 flagged this and did not measure it. Here it is (`when_table.py`): 40 maps, every *This
353	happened* on every claim, 24 slices, 200 000 worlds, against the judge — which holds the whole
354	joint over days and is therefore exact.
355	
356	*Total variation distance* below is half the sum of the absolute differences between two
357	distributions over days: 0 means identical, .10 means a tenth of the worlds would have to move.
358	
359	| how each claim's day-it-happened spread compares with the judge's | mean | 99th pct | worst |
360	|---|---|---|---|
361	| **(a) weighted forward sample** | .0023 | .0047 | **.0064** |
362	| **(b) truths from the exact solve, days drawn forward under the prior** | .0104 | .0575 | **.2143** |
363	
364	| how far the median day moves, in slices (one slice = 2.5 days) | mean | 99th pct | worst |
365	|---|---|---|---|
366	| (a) weighted forward sample | .02 | 1 | 1 |
367	| (b) truths exact, days forward | .22 | 2 | **4 (ten days)** |
368	
369	The design's own way of producing days — draw the truth pattern from the exact yes/no answer, then
370	walk the map drawing each true claim's day from tables built before the evidence — moves a claim's
371	median arrival by **up to ten days** under an observation. A stop-versus-target number computed
372	from those days is wrong by whatever ten days of path is worth. Candidate (a)'s days are right to
373	within sampling noise, and the same weighted sample serves both readers: one sampler, two uses.
374	
375	---
376	
377	## 8. The tolerance to write in the record
378	
379	For `test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time` — the test whose enumerator is forbidden the
380	core's tables and is built from the arrow parameters alone.
381	
382	**If the core is the weighted forward sample with the control variate, 200 000 worlds, 24 slices:**
383	
384	| question | measured worst over 4 480–560 numbers | write |
385	|---|---|---|
386	| no edit | .0013 | **.005** |
387	| *Suppose this is true* | .0014 | **.005** |
388	| *This happened* | .0020 | **.005** |
389	
390	At 50 000 worlds the measured worsts are `.0030`, `.0019`, `.0054`; `.005` then has no headroom on
391	*This happened* and the sample size must be part of the record.
392	
393	**If the core is the prior-timing tables as proposed, 24 slices:**
394	
395	| question | measured worst | write |
396	|---|---|---|
397	| no edit | .0175 | **.02** |
398	| *Suppose this is true* | .0259 | **.03** |
399	| *This happened* | .2043 | **.21** |
400	
401	**Two conditions on either number.** The enumerator must run at the **same number of slices and the
402	same within-slice convention** as the core; a core at 24 slices judged by an enumerator at 60 with
403	a different convention differs by `.0290` on its own, which would swallow the tolerance. And the
404	sample must be seeded, so the test is deterministic.
405	
406	---
407	
408	## 9. What the decision record must say — sentences ready to paste
409	
410	> **On what is exact.** *Suppose this is true* is exact: pin the claim, redo the forward pass, solve
411	> the yes/no network. Measured against an enumerator that integrates over the whole joint of event
412	> times, 4 480 numbers on 140 adversarial four-claim maps, the worst gap is `.0259` and 99.8% are
413	> inside `.005`.
414	
415	> **On what is not.** *This happened* is not exact. Evidence moves *when* a cause happened as well
416	> as *whether* it did, and the yes/no tables were built from the timing the map had before the
417	> evidence arrived. Measured the same way, the worst gap is `.2043` and 6.6% of numbers are off by
418	> more than `.005`. It bites when the observed claim is itself a cause of another cause and the
419	> reach is through impulse arrows; a plain chain is exact.
420	
421	> **On the cure.** *This happened* is answered by a weighted forward sample: worlds drawn forward
422	> with event days, the observed claim set to what was observed and the world weighted by how likely
423	> that was, with the exact yes/no answer used as a control variate so that only the correction is
424	> sampled. At 200 000 worlds the worst gap is `.0020` and no number is off by more than `.005`. The
425	> sample is seeded and reproducible. The same sample is what the trade reads as event days.
426	
427	> **On the day a slice stands for.** An arrival inside a slice is taken to be at the slice's
428	> **middle**, not its end. At 24 slices this changes the worst gap against a fine reference from
429	> `.0290` to `.0027`; the last-day convention at 60 slices is worse than the middle-day convention
430	> at 12.
431	
432	> **On the range.** A range is the 5th-to-95th percentile band across **2 000** versions of the map.
433	> The inner eight worlds are removed; the outer 2 000 are not. At 200 versions the band's ends
434	> wander by a tenth of the band's own width, which is one significant figure, not two.
435	
436	> **On cost, and what is not yet settled.** A twenty-claim map with up to three causes per claim and
437	> 200 versions costs 3.0 seconds for one world with its range, of which 2.9 seconds is the forward
438	> pass that builds the tables and 0.11 seconds is the sample. The 300 ms budget is not met and this
439	> record does not claim it is. The costed ways down are a coarser window (measured: 12 slices costs
440	> 2.5% of *This happened* numbers more than `.005`), fewer integration points inside each slice
441	> (measured cost only, accuracy not measured), and replacing the table enumeration with a small
442	> quadrature (measured: 64× fewer entries, and it roughly doubles the share of numbers off by more
443	> than `.005`).
444	
445	---
446	
447	## 10. What I did not check
448	
449	- **Anything above four claims, for accuracy.** The judge is not computable there. Every accuracy
450	  number in this report is from four-claim maps; the cost numbers are from twenty-claim maps and the
451	  two sets never meet.
452	- **Whether the correction stays shareable on a hard map.** The version-to-version movement of the
453	  correction was measured on eight four-claim maps where the correction is a few thousandths. On a
454	  map shaped like trial 33 the correction is `.20` and its movement across versions is unmeasured.
455	- **Fewer integration points inside a slice.** The cost was measured (one point instead of eight is
456	  4.9× faster on the table build); the accuracy was not, because the red team's calibration is fixed
457	  at eight and changing it means changing their code.
458	- **The *Suppose this is true* row of the grid comparison.** A supposition pins the claim to the
459	  first slice, whose representative day differs between grids, so that row measures the harness's
460	  pinning convention as much as the model. A real implementation pins to day zero.
461	- **A quadrature that is not stratified quantiles.** The five-point quadrature measured here is
462	  noisy in the number of points (eight points is not reliably better than three) because the points
463	  are rounded to slice indices. A better rule probably exists; I did not look for one.
464	- **A real generated map.** All maps here are synthetic, from the red team's generator and
465	  `ve_cost.layered_dag`. The one real generated map in the repository is a tree.
466	- **Anything about state claims** — their on-time and off-time, and what they cost. That is the
467	  other half of stack 05's spike and it is a different agent's subject.
468	- **The stop-versus-target number itself.** §7 measures the error in the *days*; it does not push
469	  those days through a price path to a first-touch probability.
470	- **I ran no test suite, no server, no browser and no paid call.** Nothing in the repository outside
471	  `plans/` was changed.
472	
473	---
474	
475	## Owed once stack 04 has landed
476	
477	Nothing. This spike wrote no product code and no chapter. The sentences in §9 belong to record 0016,
478	which the coordinator owns and which is not yet written.

# Spike 05-0 — how *This happened* is computed, and to what tolerance

**2026-09-21 · one read-only Opus agent · no file in the repository or any worktree was changed
outside `plans/`.** Every number below is printed by a script in
`plans/analysis/scripts/spike-05/observe/`, and the script is named beside it. The raw output of
every run is in `logs/` in that directory. No paid call, no server, no browser, no test suite.

**The words used here.** A *claim* is a yes/no proposition with a deadline; its number is the
chance it happens by that deadline. An *arrow* bends the *rate* at which its target happens from
the day its source happened plus a lag, with a shape (`step`, `impulse` with a half-life, `ramp`).
A *slice* is one of the K equal pieces the 60-day window is cut into; a claim's *arrival* is the
slice it first came true in, or "never". A *version* is one draw of the map's uncertain inputs; a
*range* is the 5th-to-95th percentile band of a number across versions. The *judge* is the exact
answer over the whole joint of arrival slices — computable only for four claims or fewer, which is
why accuracy is measured there and cost at twenty claims.

---

## The verdict in five lines

1. **Kill. No candidate passes the criterion as written**, and the binding constraint is not
   *This happened* at all — it is the forward pass that builds the tables, which all three
   candidates share and which nobody had costed. At twenty claims with two hundred versions it is
   **2.9 seconds**, against a 300 ms budget (`timing20.py`).
2. **The accuracy question has a clear winner.** A weighted forward sample with the exact yes/no
   solve used as a control variate — Kent's "exact core with a sampler on top", read literally —
   holds `.005` on **100.00%** of the adversarial set's *This happened* numbers at 200 000 worlds
   and **99.98%** at 50 000, against 93.4% for the design as proposed (`candidates.py`).
3. **Tolerance for the record:** `.005` for all three questions if the sampler lands; `.02` for no
   edit, `.03` for *Suppose this is true* and `.21` for *This happened* if the prior-timing tables
   are kept as they are.
4. **Versions per range: 2 000 is right, and only for narrow bands.** At the widths these maps
   produce, 2 000 versions still leaves the worst band end wandering `.0086`; 200 versions leaves
   it wandering `.0275`, which is one significant figure, not two (`versions.py`).
5. **Two findings worth more than the spike's own question.** Representing an arrival by the
   *middle* of its slice rather than its *end* — one line — cuts the grid error at 24 slices from
   a worst of `.0290` to `.0027` (`midpoint.py`). And the 0.5 ms that the engine design was sold on
   measured the elimination only: the factors were built from a random logistic function before the
   clock started (`analysis/scripts/engine/ve_cost.py:238-239`, clock at `:205`, factors at `:135`).

---

## 1. The baseline reproduces, digit for digit

The red team's own script was re-run unmodified, and the same sweep was re-run through this
spike's faster code. Both give the red team's table exactly.

**140 adversarial four-claim maps (seed 7), 17 queries each, 24 slices, arrival at the slice's
last day.** Gap between the design as proposed and the judge.

| query | numbers | mean | 99th percentile | worst | share off by more than .005 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no edit | 560 | .00027 | .0046 | .0175 | 0.9% |
| *Suppose this is true* | 4 480 | .00007 | .0015 | .0259 | 0.2% |
| *This happened* | 4 480 | .00127 | .0151 | **.2043** | **6.6%** |

Worst single number: trial 33, *This happened* on `c1`, read on `c3` — judge `.6155`, design
`.4112`.

*From `logs/baseline-redteam-attack2.log` (the red team's `attack2.py`, untouched) and
`logs/baseline.log` (`baseline.py`).*

**The faster code is the same code.** `spike_core.judge` shares each map's tables across its 17
queries instead of rebuilding them per query; `selfcheck.py` runs both side by side on 12 maps ×
17 queries and reports a worst difference of **0.000e+00** against `rt_core.exact_over_times` and
**1.6e-11** against `rt_core.binary`, at 167× the speed. Nothing in the red team's directory was
edited.

---

## 2. The candidates

All on the same 140 maps, 24 slices, judged against exact-over-times. The *This happened* column
is the one the criterion is about; `logs/candidates.log`, `logs/perday.log`.

### (a) A weighted forward sample — `sampler.py`

Worlds are drawn forward with arrival days, causes first. At the observed claim the world is not
thrown away: the claim is set to what was observed and the world's weight is multiplied by how
likely that was. Three variance reductions, all on: conditional sampling at the evidence, so no
world is wasted; the exact yes/no solve as a control variate — the same world is drawn twice, once
under the full time model and once under the design's own yes/no model, using the same random
number for each claim, so only the *difference* has to be sampled and it is added to an answer we
already know exactly; and one seeded stream in a fixed claim order, so two runs agree.

| *This happened*, 4 480 numbers | mean | 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| read straight off the worlds, 50 000 | .00120 | .0051 | .0076 | 1.18% |
| read straight off the worlds, 200 000 | .00060 | .0026 | .0049 | 0.00% |
| **with the control variate, 50 000** | .00029 | .0021 | .0054 | **0.02%** |
| **with the control variate, 200 000** | .00015 | .0011 | .0020 | **0.00%** |
| with the control variate, 1 000 000 | .00007 | .0005 | .0011 | 0.00% |

It fixes the other two questions as well, because it targets the judge rather than the tables:

| | no edit (560) | *Suppose* (4 480) |
|---|---|---|
| the design's tables | worst .0175, 0.89% over .005 | worst .0259, 0.22% over .005 |
| sample + control variate, 50 000 | worst .0030, 0.00% | worst .0019, 0.00% |
| sample + control variate, 200 000 | worst .0013, 0.00% | worst .0014, 0.00% |

**Effective sample size** — how many equally-weighted worlds the weighted sample is worth — is
**96.7%** of the worlds drawn on average and **41.8%** at its worst across all 1 120 observations.
On the twenty-claim map it is 161 044 of 200 000 at 12 slices and 164 430 at 24
(`timing20.py`). The control variate buys a factor of about 2.4 on the 99th percentile, no more:
the two coupled worlds disagree 6.3% of the time on the hardest map, which is where the residual
variance lives (`probe_sampler.py`).

**Cost with a range (20 claims):** 190 ms for 200 000 worlds over all twenty claims at 12 slices,
**110 ms** over the twelve claims the evidence can reach (a claim cut off from the evidence keeps
its number exactly and need not be drawn — `engine20.reach_submap`). At 24 slices, 380 ms and
222 ms. That is *per version*, unless the correction is shared — see §5.

### (b) Accept the prior-timing tables — `spike_core.candidate_b`

The design as proposed, unchanged. Its honest tolerance is the baseline table in §1: **.02 for no
edit, .03 for *Suppose this is true*, .21 for *This happened***. A screen that prints two
significant figures beside `.21` of possible error on its second verb is printing a digit it does
not have. 6.63% of *This happened* numbers are off by more than `.005`, 0.56% by more than `.02`,
and 0.04% by more than `.05` (`tails.py`).

### (c) Re-cut the yes/no variable — `perday.py`, `hybrid.py`

Two readings were built, because the brief's phrase admits both.

**Per evidence day** (`perday.py`) — the literal reading. Answer the question once for each
possible day of the observed claim: pin that day, redo the forward pass, rebuild every table
downstream, solve; weight each answer by the likelihood of that day, which falls out of the solve.

**Widened variables** (`hybrid.py`) — give some claims their whole arrival slice as a variable
(K+1 values) instead of a yes/no. With nothing widened this is the design; with everything widened
it is the judge. Three rules were tried: widen only the observed claim; widen it and everything
upstream; widen everything the evidence can reach that some other claim reads.

| *This happened*, 4 480 numbers | mean | 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| widen only the observed claim | .00119 | .0144 | .1968 | 5.98% |
| **per evidence day** | .00086 | .0127 | .0680 | 4.38% |
| widen it and its causes | .00040 | .0080 | .1963 | 1.85% |
| **widen everything the evidence reaches that is read** | .00002 | .0006 | .0063 | **0.07%** |

Only the last passes, and on a four-claim map it widens three claims of four — that is the judge
with one sink left over. Its cost is therefore the cost already measured and rejected for exact
inference over event times (`analysis/2026-09-21-digest-engine.md`: 0.7–7.8 s per range at twenty
claims). On the twenty-claim map measured here it widened only 5 of 20 claims and cost 25 ms per
version, but that is an accident of where the observation sat: `c6`'s only descendants are sinks,
which nobody reads. An observation higher up the map widens most of it.

**The per-day version can be worse than doing nothing.** On trial 65 it takes `c3` from the
design's `.5261` to `.4872` against a judge of `.5553` — it fixes the observed claim's own day and
leaves its *causes'* days alone, and the two errors stop cancelling (`worst_case.py`).

---

## 3. The kill criterion, applied literally

> *A candidate passes if it holds `.005` on 99% of the adversarial set **and** runs inside 300 ms
> on a 20-claim map (up to 3 causes per claim) for one world with its range.*

**Accuracy.** Passes: (a) with the control variate at 50 000 worlds or more (99.98%); (c) widened
to everything the evidence reaches (99.93%). Fails: (b) the tables as proposed (93.4%); (c) per
evidence day (95.6%); (c) with the smaller widenings.

**Milliseconds.** `timing20.py`, on a map from `ve_cost.layered_dag(20, 3, seed=1000)`, one
observation in force, all twenty marginals. The first three rows are the *shared* pass every
candidate pays for before anyone asks a question.

| | 1 version | 50 | 100 | 200 | 2 000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| calibrate the arrows | 28.0 | 95 | 192 | 384 | 3 905 |
| build the conditional tables | 12.9 | 628 | 1 217 | 2 438 | 24 831 |
| forward pass + yes/no tables | 0.9 | 14 | 28 | 56 | 570 |
| **shared by every candidate** | **41.8** | **737** | **1 437** | **2 879** | **29 318** |
| the exact yes/no solve, all marginals | 4.4 | 6.4 | 8.7 | 12.4 | 83 |
| **(b) total** | **46 ✓** | 744 | 1 446 | **2 891** | 29 401 |
| **(a) total, correction shared** | **161 ✓** | 856 | 1 555 | **3 002** | 29 527 |
| (a) total, correction redone per version | 161 ✓ | 6 367 | 12 340 | 24 992 | 281 761 |
| (c) per evidence day, every version | 101 ✓ | 3 709 | 7 406 | 14 611 | 152 022 |

*All milliseconds, 12 slices, eight integration points per slice. ✓ = inside 300 ms.*

At 24 slices — which §4 shows is the coarsest window worth having — the shared pass alone is
**208 ms for one version** and **9.6 s for fifty**.

**So: no candidate passes.** The nearest miss is candidate (a) with the correction shared across
versions: **3.0 s at 200 versions and 12 slices, ten times the budget**. And the miss is not in the
sampler, which is 110 ms; it is in the 2.9 s of table-building that candidate (b) pays too.

**What relaxing the criterion buys.**

| relaxation | what it buys | what it costs |
|---|---|---|
| budget **3 s** for one world with its range | (a) passes at 12 slices, 200 versions | 12 slices is 2.5% of *This happened* numbers off by more than .005 against the continuous answer, even with the middle-day fix (§4) — so the accuracy half then fails |
| budget **12 s** | (a) passes at 24 slices, 200 versions, with both halves honest | a range takes twelve seconds |
| accuracy **.02 on 99%** | (b) passes accuracy: its 99th percentiles are .0046 / .0015 / .0151 | nothing on the clock — (b) is still 2.9 s at 200 versions. Relaxing accuracy alone does not help |
| **50 versions** instead of 200 | shared pass falls to 737 ms | the band's ends wander `.0498` — one significant figure |
| **one claim's number at a time**, no range | 46 ms (b) / 161 ms (a) — both pass | there is no range, which is the product's honesty feature |

**The cheapest thing that has not been tried.** The tables are built by enumerating every
combination of the causes' arrival slices — 2 006 900 entries for this map at 24 slices — and then
*averaging* them. An average does not need every point. Replacing the enumeration with five
quadrature points per cause cuts it to 31 375 entries (64× fewer) and the whole forward pass from
208 ms to **38.5 ms** per version. It costs accuracy: *This happened* goes from 5.68% to 9.27% off
by more than .005, and no edit from 1.25% to 2.92% (`quad.py`, 60 maps). **And it is not available
to the winning candidate**, because a weighted forward sample needs a claim's table at whatever day
its causes actually landed on, not at five chosen days.

---

## 4. The grid nobody chose — the largest single number in this report

Every measurement above compares candidates *on the same grid*, so it is a fair comparison. But the
grid itself carries an error that the judge and every candidate share, and it is bigger than the
thing this spike was sent to measure.

A cause that arrives anywhere inside a slice has to be given a day. `rt_core` gives it the slice's
**last** day. That is late by half a slice on average — 1.25 days at 24 slices on a 60-day window.

Against a fine reference (60 slices, middle day), 10 maps, every query (`convergence.py`,
`midpoint.py`):

| the engine's window | *This happened*: 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 slices, arrival at the slice's last day | .0547 | .0668 | 44.7% |
| 24 slices, last day | .0240 | .0290 | 27.8% |
| 60 slices, last day | .0093 | .0111 | 8.1% |
| **12 slices, arrival at the slice's middle** | .0068 | .0085 | 2.5% |
| **24 slices, middle** | **.0018** | **.0027** | **0.00%** |

**Twelve slices with the middle-day convention beats sixty slices with the last-day one, at a
twentieth of the cost.** This is a one-line change (`spike_core.representative_days`) and it costs
nothing.

It does **not** change which candidate wins. Re-run at 24 slices, middle day, judged there
(`midpoint.py`, 140 maps): the design's tables are still 6.07% off by more than .005 on *This
happened*, worst `.2095`; the sample with the control variate is still 0.00%, worst `.0021`. The
two defects are independent, and both are real.

*One caveat, honestly.* The *Suppose this is true* row of the grid comparison (5.6% over .005 at 24
slices middle day) is an artefact of this harness, not of the model: a supposition pins the claim
to the first slice, whose representative day differs between grids. A real implementation would pin
it to day zero. It is listed under what I did not check.

---

## 5. The worst remaining case, drawn

Trial 33 of the adversarial set is where the design is worst, and it is exactly the shape the red
team named: the observed claim is also a cause of another cause, and the reach is through impulse
arrows (`worst_case.py`).

```
   c0  ── deadline day 8.5, own chance .54
    │
    ├──► c1  deadline day 20.3, own chance .07
    │        from c0: .11 if that cause alone happens, lag 5.2 d, step
    │
    ├──► c2  deadline day 43.4, own chance .10
    │        from c0: .61, lag 3.1 d, step
    │        from c1: .33, lag 2.5 d, IMPULSE half-life 5.7 d
    │
    └──► c3  deadline day 56.0, own chance .09
             from c0: .11, lag 18.2 d, IMPULSE half-life 4.6 d
             from c2: .91, lag  5.2 d, IMPULSE half-life 12.4 d
             from c1: .03, lag 16.1 d, IMPULSE half-life 13.5 d
```

*This happened: `c1` is true.*

| | c0 | c1 | c2 | **c3** | worst gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| judge (exact over times) | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | **.6155** | — |
| (b) prior-timing tables | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7269 | **.4112** | **.2043** |
| (c) widen the observed claim | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7282 | .4187 | .1968 |
| (c) widen it and its causes | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | .4192 | .1963 |
| (c) per evidence day | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7282 | .6076 | .0079 |
| (c) widen everything read | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | .6155 | .0000 |
| (a) sample 200 000, corrected | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7278 | .6159 | **.0005** |

Twenty points of probability, on the claim furthest downstream — the kind of claim a trade sits on.
The design prints `.41` where the answer is `.62`.

**The worst case candidate (a) has left** is not structural: trial 21, *This happened* on `c0`, read
on `c2` — judge `.4807`, sample `.4821`, gap `.0020` at 200 000 worlds, and it shrinks as the square
root of the count. **The worst case candidate (c) widened has left** is trial 124, gap `.0063`, and
it does not shrink with anything.

---

## 6. How many versions a range needs

`versions.py`. Twenty thousand versions of the twenty-claim map are solved exactly under an
observation; that pool stands in for "all versions". Then each smaller count is drawn from it two
thousand times and the band recomputed. *Wander* is half the middle 90% of where an end lands.

**Uncertain inputs drawn wide (a typical band .254 across):**

| versions | worst end wanders | as a share of the band | share of band ends inside .005 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | .0498 | 18% | 22.9% |
| 100 | .0390 | 14% | 29.6% |
| 200 | .0275 | 10% | 38.8% |
| 500 | .0176 | 6% | 55.6% |
| **2 000** | **.0086** | **3%** | **83.9%** |

**Uncertain inputs drawn narrow (a typical band .115 across):**

| versions | worst end wanders | as a share of the band | share inside .005 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | .0252 | 16% | 41.0% |
| 100 | .0192 | 12% | 53.0% |
| 200 | .0133 | 9% | 67.7% |
| 500 | .0086 | 6% | 86.5% |
| **2 000** | **.0046** | **3%** | **99.2%** |

**Recommendation: keep 2 000.** It is the smallest count that holds a narrow band's ends to two
significant figures, and even it does not hold a wide band's — a band `.25` across needs about
**6 000** versions for that, by the square-root rule the table obeys. The engine analyst's proposal
of "about 200 versions" is **wrong by an order of magnitude**: at 200 versions the 5th and 95th
ends wander by a tenth of the band's own width, which is one significant figure. The inner eight
worlds do go away — that saving is real — but it does not buy a smaller outer loop.

**Can the correction for *This happened* be shared across versions?** Yes, and it is the only thing
that makes candidate (a) affordable at all. On 8 maps × 200 versions, with the exact correction
(judge minus the design's answer) computed per version:

| | mean | 90th pct | worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| how big the correction is | .0005 | .0019 | .0041 |
| how much it moves from version to version (sd) | .0008 | .0025 | .0071 |
| how much the answer itself moves (sd) | .0616 | .1107 | .1234 |
| the ratio of those two | .011 | .030 | .096 |

The correction moves about **1% as much as the answer does**. Sharing one sampled correction across
every version adds about `.0013` to a band end on average and `.0117` at its worst. That is the
trade: one sample instead of two hundred, for a hundredth of an extra error on most numbers and a
tail that needs watching on maps where the correction is large. **These eight maps are four claims
each and the correction is small on them by construction** — on a map shaped like trial 33 the
correction is `.20`, and 1% of that is `.002`, still small, but nobody has measured the version-to-
version movement of a correction that size.

**Cost per version, and therefore per range** (candidate (a), 12 slices, shared correction):
2 879 ms of shared pass + 12 ms of solve for 200 versions + 110 ms for one sample = **3 002 ms**.
Per version that is 14.4 ms, and the sample is a fixed 110 ms however many versions there are.

---

## 7. The times the trade will read

Stack 06 reads a sample of worlds as `when` (the day each claim first came true, −1 for never) plus
a `weight`. Under *This happened* those days are only right if whatever produced them is. Red team
S2 flagged this and did not measure it. Here it is (`when_table.py`): 40 maps, every *This
happened* on every claim, 24 slices, 200 000 worlds, against the judge — which holds the whole
joint over days and is therefore exact.

*Total variation distance* below is half the sum of the absolute differences between two
distributions over days: 0 means identical, .10 means a tenth of the worlds would have to move.

| how each claim's day-it-happened spread compares with the judge's | mean | 99th pct | worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(a) weighted forward sample** | .0023 | .0047 | **.0064** |
| **(b) truths from the exact solve, days drawn forward under the prior** | .0104 | .0575 | **.2143** |

| how far the median day moves, in slices (one slice = 2.5 days) | mean | 99th pct | worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) weighted forward sample | .02 | 1 | 1 |
| (b) truths exact, days forward | .22 | 2 | **4 (ten days)** |

The design's own way of producing days — draw the truth pattern from the exact yes/no answer, then
walk the map drawing each true claim's day from tables built before the evidence — moves a claim's
median arrival by **up to ten days** under an observation. A stop-versus-target number computed
from those days is wrong by whatever ten days of path is worth. Candidate (a)'s days are right to
within sampling noise, and the same weighted sample serves both readers: one sampler, two uses.

---

## 8. The tolerance to write in the record

For `test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time` — the test whose enumerator is forbidden the
core's tables and is built from the arrow parameters alone.

**If the core is the weighted forward sample with the control variate, 200 000 worlds, 24 slices:**

| question | measured worst over 4 480–560 numbers | write |
|---|---|---|
| no edit | .0013 | **.005** |
| *Suppose this is true* | .0014 | **.005** |
| *This happened* | .0020 | **.005** |

At 50 000 worlds the measured worsts are `.0030`, `.0019`, `.0054`; `.005` then has no headroom on
*This happened* and the sample size must be part of the record.

**If the core is the prior-timing tables as proposed, 24 slices:**

| question | measured worst | write |
|---|---|---|
| no edit | .0175 | **.02** |
| *Suppose this is true* | .0259 | **.03** |
| *This happened* | .2043 | **.21** |

**Two conditions on either number.** The enumerator must run at the **same number of slices and the
same within-slice convention** as the core; a core at 24 slices judged by an enumerator at 60 with
a different convention differs by `.0290` on its own, which would swallow the tolerance. And the
sample must be seeded, so the test is deterministic.

---

## 9. What the decision record must say — sentences ready to paste

> **On what is exact.** *Suppose this is true* is exact: pin the claim, redo the forward pass, solve
> the yes/no network. Measured against an enumerator that integrates over the whole joint of event
> times, 4 480 numbers on 140 adversarial four-claim maps, the worst gap is `.0259` and 99.8% are
> inside `.005`.

> **On what is not.** *This happened* is not exact. Evidence moves *when* a cause happened as well
> as *whether* it did, and the yes/no tables were built from the timing the map had before the
> evidence arrived. Measured the same way, the worst gap is `.2043` and 6.6% of numbers are off by
> more than `.005`. It bites when the observed claim is itself a cause of another cause and the
> reach is through impulse arrows; a plain chain is exact.

> **On the cure.** *This happened* is answered by a weighted forward sample: worlds drawn forward
> with event days, the observed claim set to what was observed and the world weighted by how likely
> that was, with the exact yes/no answer used as a control variate so that only the correction is
> sampled. At 200 000 worlds the worst gap is `.0020` and no number is off by more than `.005`. The
> sample is seeded and reproducible. The same sample is what the trade reads as event days.

> **On the day a slice stands for.** An arrival inside a slice is taken to be at the slice's
> **middle**, not its end. At 24 slices this changes the worst gap against a fine reference from
> `.0290` to `.0027`; the last-day convention at 60 slices is worse than the middle-day convention
> at 12.

> **On the range.** A range is the 5th-to-95th percentile band across **2 000** versions of the map.
> The inner eight worlds are removed; the outer 2 000 are not. At 200 versions the band's ends
> wander by a tenth of the band's own width, which is one significant figure, not two.

> **On cost, and what is not yet settled.** A twenty-claim map with up to three causes per claim and
> 200 versions costs 3.0 seconds for one world with its range, of which 2.9 seconds is the forward
> pass that builds the tables and 0.11 seconds is the sample. The 300 ms budget is not met and this
> record does not claim it is. The costed ways down are a coarser window (measured: 12 slices costs
> 2.5% of *This happened* numbers more than `.005`), fewer integration points inside each slice
> (measured cost only, accuracy not measured), and replacing the table enumeration with a small
> quadrature (measured: 64× fewer entries, and it roughly doubles the share of numbers off by more
> than `.005`).

---

## 10. What I did not check

- **Anything above four claims, for accuracy.** The judge is not computable there. Every accuracy
  number in this report is from four-claim maps; the cost numbers are from twenty-claim maps and the
  two sets never meet.
- **Whether the correction stays shareable on a hard map.** The version-to-version movement of the
  correction was measured on eight four-claim maps where the correction is a few thousandths. On a
  map shaped like trial 33 the correction is `.20` and its movement across versions is unmeasured.
- **Fewer integration points inside a slice.** The cost was measured (one point instead of eight is
  4.9× faster on the table build); the accuracy was not, because the red team's calibration is fixed
  at eight and changing it means changing their code.
- **The *Suppose this is true* row of the grid comparison.** A supposition pins the claim to the
  first slice, whose representative day differs between grids, so that row measures the harness's
  pinning convention as much as the model. A real implementation pins to day zero.
- **A quadrature that is not stratified quantiles.** The five-point quadrature measured here is
  noisy in the number of points (eight points is not reliably better than three) because the points
  are rounded to slice indices. A better rule probably exists; I did not look for one.
- **A real generated map.** All maps here are synthetic, from the red team's generator and
  `ve_cost.layered_dag`. The one real generated map in the repository is a tree.
- **Anything about state claims** — their on-time and off-time, and what they cost. That is the
  other half of stack 05's spike and it is a different agent's subject.
- **The stop-versus-target number itself.** §7 measures the error in the *days*; it does not push
  those days through a price path to a first-touch probability.
- **I ran no test suite, no server, no browser and no paid call.** Nothing in the repository outside
  `plans/` was changed.

---

## Owed once stack 04 has landed

Nothing. This spike wrote no product code and no chapter. The sentences in §9 belong to record 0016,
which the coordinator owns and which is not yet written.
